query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultra-thin, well-adhered lanthanum oxide (La2O3) coating onto boride-based components will significantly improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by forming a stable, protective barrier that also exhibits self-healing behavior upon reaction with the molten aluminum.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components currently used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that are uncoated or conventionally treated and experience rapid degradation from molten aluminum exposure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a surface modification by applying an ultra-thin La2O3 coating using a controlled sol–gel or physical vapor deposition process.
generation.conditions: The intervention is designed to be effective under standard hot-dip aluminum plating conditions (approximately 650–750°C) with molten aluminum compositions having impurity levels typical of industrial settings and during extended immersion periods simulating actual processing cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: The La2O3 layer acts as a physical barrier against aluminum ion ingress and, upon contact with molten aluminum, forms a self-healing interface that preferentially reacts with corrosive species, thereby protecting the underlying boride substrate.
generation.mechanism: Due to its high thermodynamic stability and barrier properties at elevated temperatures, the lanthanum oxide coating limits the direct diffusion and chemical attack of molten aluminum on the boride surface. Its dynamic self-healing behavior is expected to continuously repair minor disruptions in the barrier, maintaining its integrity during exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated boride components, La2O3-coated samples are predicted to exhibit at least a 50% reduction in corrosion rate, as measured by weight loss and depth of attack during standardized molten aluminum immersion tests.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components with no specialized surface treatment or only conventional treatments that fail to form a robust, adherent barrier against molten aluminum.
generation.boundary: This protective effect is expected to hold under high-temperature molten aluminum exposure (650–750°C) with typical industrial impurity ranges and for durations that mimic operational conditions; deviations in temperature, extreme impurity levels, or mechanical stress may challenge the coating’s integrity.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of corrosion rate reduction and the long-term adherence of the ultrathin La2O3 coating under repeated thermal cycles and mechanical stresses remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of boride-based component samples: one group coated with a uniform, ultra-thin La2O3 layer using controlled sol–gel or PVD methods, and an uncoated control group. Immerse both groups into molten aluminum maintained at 650–750°C under identical conditions for a duration representative of actual plating processes.
measurements: Weight loss measurements before and after immersion
Cross-sectional microstructural analysis using SEM/EDS to assess the depth and nature of corrosion attack
Phase identification via XRD to confirm the presence and integrity of the La2O3 barrier and any reaction products
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the La2O3-coated samples do not demonstrate at least a 50% improvement (i.e., a reduction in weight loss or penetration depth) in corrosion resistance relative to the uncoated controls, or if the coating exhibits failure (e.g., delamination or excessive degradation) under the test conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. frame.system: Boride-based components in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that are directly exposed to molten aluminum environments.
frame.goal: Improve the molten-aluminum corrosion resistance of the boride-based components relative to the current untreated or conventionally treated baseline.
frame.limitation: The components currently suffer from rapid degradation due to the aggressive corrosive attack by molten aluminum.
constraints: The intervention must have a defined mechanism of action and measurable improvement relative to the baseline
It must remain effective under the operating conditions of molten aluminum plating
frame.regime: High-temperature environment where components are in direct contact with molten aluminum (typically in the range of 650–750°C) during the hot-dip plating process.
prior_attempts: Previous approaches have included microstructural refinement and altering the bulk alloy composition of boride-based components or attempting thicker oxide layers. These methods fell short due to insufficient adhesion or inadequate barrier performance under the severe conditions of molten aluminum contact.
frame.understanding: A better protective barrier mechanism is needed to inhibit molten-aluminum attack. The intervention should not only passivate the surface but also maintain its integrity at high temperatures.
frame.proposed_intervention: Introduce a surface modification wherein an ultra-thin, well-adhered lanthanum oxide (La2O3) coating is applied onto the boride-based component via a controlled sol–gel or physical vapor deposition process. The La2O3 layer is hypothesized to serve dual functions: (1) acting as a stable physical barrier at high temperatures to slow the diffusion of aluminum ions, and (2) chemically interacting with the molten aluminum to form a self-healing interface that preferentially consumes corrosive species before they attack the underlying boride substrate.
frame.mechanism: Lanthanum oxide, due to its high thermodynamic stability and barrier properties, can reduce the direct interaction between molten aluminum and the boride surface. Its potential to form a dynamically self-healing surface layer, when exposed to the reactive environment, limits the penetration of aluminum, thereby reducing corrosion.
frame.predicted_improvement: Relative to an untreated boride-based component, the La2O3-coated variant is predicted to exhibit at least a 50% reduction in corrosion rate (e.g., measured as weight loss or depth of attack) during standardized molten aluminum immersion tests.
frame.conditions_of_effectiveness: The protective effect is expected to remain effective under typical aluminum plating temperatures (approximately 650–750°C), for molten aluminum compositions with impurity levels within standard industrial ranges, and during prolonged exposure that mimics actual processing conditions.
frame.supporting_prior_evidence: Previous studies in high-temperature corrosion environments have shown that rare-earth oxide coatings, such as La2O3, provide improved oxidation and corrosion resistance in metal-ceramic systems, suggesting a similar beneficial role when applied to boride-based substrates.
frame.experimental_design: A controlled experiment could involve preparing two sets of boride-based samples: one set coated with the La2O3 film and one uncoated (baseline). Both sets would be immersed in molten aluminum under identical conditions (temperature, immersion time, and aluminum composition). The performance metric would be the rate of corrosion measured by weight loss, cross-sectional microstructural analysis (using SEM/EDS), and phase identification via XRD. A statistically significant lower degradation in the coated samples compared to the baseline would support the hypothesis; conversely, similar or worse performance would falsify it.

decision.trend: Earlier work on improving high‐temperature resistance in harsh environments initially focused on modifying the bulk alloy composition or creating thicker oxide layers to protect substrates. However, these strategies proved limited because the engineered oxides did not adhere well or failed to act as an effective barrier under aggressive high-temperature contacts. In addition, studies that improved oxidation resistance through surface-focused treatments (for example, silicide coatings in PMC11077685) indicate that a more nuanced surface or interface engineering approach can be effective.
decision.unsolved: The open challenge remains to create a protective, adherent, and thermodynamically stable barrier that not only passivates the surface but also dynamically interacts with the molten aluminum environment. Bulk modifications or simply thickening oxide scales have fallen short because they cannot maintain integrity and adhesion under prolonged high-temperature exposure in molten aluminum.
decision.lever: application of an ultra-thin, well-adhered lanthanum oxide (La2O3) coating via controlled sol–gel or physical vapor deposition processes
decision.why: The trend shows a shift from less effective bulk and oxide-layer modifications to targeted surface modifications that better form protective barriers under severe conditions. Lanthanum oxide is known for its high thermodynamic stability and barrier properties at elevated temperatures, and its capacity to form a self-healing interface is a compelling mechanism to inhibit molten aluminum attack. This approach directly addresses the known limitations by focusing on surface integrity and adhesion, and it follows logically from the previous successes in surface-treated systems.
